 The Rundown: Illinois voters hit the polls
 Plus, the Northern Illinois Transit Authority’s expanded budget. Here’s what you need to know today.
 By  
 Bianca Cseke

 Good afternoon! It’s Tuesday — and Election Day. Here’s what you need to know. 
 1. Illinois voters hit the polls with congressional power in the air on Election Day 
 As my colleagues Tina Sfondeles and Mitchell Armentrout write, today’s midterm elections will help determine control of Congress and serve as a litmus test of President Donald Trump’s far-reaching second term. The results also will help determine the trajectory of his final two years in office, with Democrats potentially regaining the ability to block or at least stall the president’s agenda.
 While reliably blue Illinois isn’t likely to shape the national picture, voters are weighing in on Gov. JB Pritzker’s bid for a third term and Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton’s fight for U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin’s seat, which hasn’t been open since 1996. The election marks the culmination of a generational shift in Illinois politics that began with Durbin’s retirement announcement in April 2025.
 Stratton, who faces former Illinois Republican Party chair Don Tracy, would become the state’s second Black woman senator and the sixth Black woman to serve in the U.S. Senate if she wins.
 Durbin wasn’t the only longtime member of Congress on the way out. U.S. Reps. Danny Davis, Jan Schakowsky and Jesus “Chuy” Garcia also announced their retirements. That means Illinois’ congressional delegation is also entering a new phase, with five new members joining the fray.
 Meanwhile, Chicagoans have their first opportunity to seat a fully elected Board of Education. The three-way race for board president among former principal Jessica Biggs, former teacher Hilario Dominguez and attorney Victor Henderson has drawn millions of dollars in outside spending seeking to influence leadership of Chicago Public Schools. [ Chicago Sun-Times ]
 You can listen to live local and national coverage and analysis beginning when polls close at 7 p.m. on WBEZ.org and 91.5 FM. And follow along here as races are called. Still haven’t voted and need to do some last-minute research? Our Voter Guide is here for you. [ WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times ]
 2. A loophole in an Illinois contract allows ICE to access data for immigration enforcement 
 The state’s victim-notification system, known as VINE, alerts crime victims when someone is released from jail, transferred or experiences a change in custody status. Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul signed the current contract with Appriss in May 2021, initially committing approximately $6.07 million. The contract runs through June 2028.
 A clause in that agreement allows Appriss to share jail records with third parties, my colleague Alma Campos reports. Privacy advocates warn this creates a pathway for information collected by Illinois jails to enter commercial databases used by U.S. Immigration & Customs Enforcement to identify and locate people.
 Illinois’ sanctuary laws limit state and local law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration authorities— including sharing information about anyone held at a local jail or prison — unless that person has a federal criminal warrant. But advocates say even though the state isn’t sharing this information directly, the loophole in the state’s contract offers a back door around the sanctuary laws.
 “This is why we’ve been raising alarms for years,” Jacinta González, a former policy director at Mijente who is now head of programs at MediaJustice, told the Chicago Sun-Times in June. “When these loopholes are allowed to exist, they’re going to lead to concrete harm. They’re going to lead to people being detained and people being deported. [ Chicago Sun-Times ]
 3. NITA’s $5 billion budget proposal boosts bus and rail frequency, as well as safety commitments 
 The Northern Illinois Transit Authority wants your input on its expanded 2027 budget that aims to improve service and safety on CTA, Metra and Pace, my colleague David Struett reports. NITA’s proposed operating budget is 15% larger than the current year — $5.02 billion compared to $4.3 billion — thanks to additional tax revenue from the NITA Act.
 This is NITA’s first time proposing its own budget for the transit agencies it now oversees. Under the Regional Transportation Authority, which NITA replaced in September, the agencies proposed their own budgets. Now, NITA is taking the lead in budgeting to better coordinate bus and rail service.
 Next year’s budget includes adding trained customer service representatives, a CTA pilot adding high-barrier gates to combat fare evasion, continued funding for more police, private security and social services, and no fare increases. Several CTA, PACE and Metra lines will see more frequent service; you can see the full list in the link.
 The draft budget is available online at nita.illinois.gov/ and open for public comment through Dec. 4. NITA will hold several public hearings, including at their Nov. 14 board hearing in the Loop. The NITA board plans to vote on a final budget Dec. 10. [ Chicago Sun-Times ]
 4. Rabbi Capers Funnye, Michelle Obama’s cousin who ran a South Side synagogue and broke racial barriers, died at 74 
 As my colleague Mitch Dudek reports, Funnye Jr. was the chief rabbi of Beth Shalom B’nai Zaken Ethiopian Hebrew Congregation on the Southwest Side, one of the largest black synagogues in America. He was credited with serving as a bridge between mainstream, mostly white, Jews and the smaller community of Black Jewish congregations.
 “Not everybody wants to be a bridge, but for Capers, he did want to do this, and was very dedicated to the work,” said Robin Washington, a co-founder in 1995, along with Rabbi Funnye, of the Alliance of Black Jews. “The Alliance only lasted for a few years, but we got the word out that Black Jews exist.”
 A celebration of life is scheduled for 10 a.m. on Friday at Beth Shalom B’nai Zaken Ethiopian Hebrew Congregation, located at 6601 S. Kedzie Ave. [ Chicago Sun-Times ]
 5. Inspired by Frank Lloyd Wright, then wronged by neglect, South Park Terrace heads for auction 
 The 121-year-old South Side Prairie School-style courtyard building featured in a 1995 Halle Berry movie is set to be auctioned off Nov. 16-18, according to a marketing brochure by Frontline Real Estate Partners.
 The opening bid is $100,000, but the real estate company expects the building to go for more than that amount, Chicago Sun-Times architecture columnist Lee Bey reports.
 Frontline was named South Park Terrace’s court-appointed receiver, after the building was vacated under city order last year due to its dilapidated condition. Officials saw the situation as exigent enough that residents had to begin leaving the building with just two days’ notice.
 The Chicago Department of Buildings said in a statement at the time that the owners, listed then as Brooklyn, New York’s 6116 MLK, “completely abandoned the building, allowing the property to go into foreclosure, and conditions continued to deteriorate to the point of imminent danger to the community.” [ Chicago Sun-Times ]
 Here’s what else is happening 
 Chicago expanded its free composting program to eight more library branches, bringing the total number of food scrap drop-off locations to 40. [ Block Club Chicago ]
 Ready or not, the holidays are rapidly approaching. Case in point: Metra announced this year’s holiday train schedule. [ WTTW ]
 Many Affordable Care Act premiums will see double-digit increases next year, with older adults most affected. [ New York Times ]
 Here are some new books to check out this month. (I’m especially interested in “Stations” and “Whale Harbor.”) [ NPR ]
 Oh, and one more thing … 
 Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became the first Black man to win boxing’s heavyweight championship, is buried at Graceland Cemetery in Uptown. In a place known for elaborate shrines to the city’s most famous, his grave went six decades without any individual marker — only a single tombstone for his family’s plot reading “Johnson.” Following the 2005 release of Ken Burns’ documentary “Unforgivable Blackness,” a small flat stone was placed to single Johnson out and note his historic achievement.
 The modesty of his burial site doesn’t reflect the man’s personality, Chicago Sun-Times contributor Steven Oxman writes: “Johnson was full of swagger and fond of fast cars and furs. His biggest victories against white champions followed with riots. There’s something about the bareness of the sport of boxing that made its champion an emblem of raw physical superiority, making the ring an arena in which racial identity felt raw and significant.”
 The tension between the ambition of excellence and fear of the consequences surrounding African American accomplishment becomes the core theme of Marco Ramirez’s play “The Royale,” inspired by Johnson’s ascent to the boxing crown and receiving a revival at Writers Theatre under the direction of Definition Theatre founder Tyrone Phillips. The work runs through Nov. 29. [ Chicago Sun-Times ]
 Tell me something good … 
 What’s something that brought you joy recently?
 Jen writes:
 “What brought me joy was sitting in an outdoor hot tub last week, on an unseasonably warm October night, with 4 fabulous girlfriends and an amazing skyline view. ❤️”
 Feel free to email me, and your response may be included in the newsletter this week.
